intro: Most of what people do on Ethereum involves tokens — stablecoins, governance tokens, NFTs, in-game items. A token is nothing mysterious: it's just a smart contract that keeps a ledger of who owns what, using the patterns you've already learned. What makes tokens work across the whole ecosystem is standards: shared interfaces that every wallet, exchange, and app agrees to speak. This lesson explains what a token really is, the two standards you must know — ERC-20 and ERC-721 — and why you should almost never write one from scratch.
objectives: Explain that a token is a contract tracking ownership, not a coin that 'moves'
Describe the ERC-20 fungible-token interface and what each function does
Explain how ERC-721 represents unique, non-fungible tokens (NFTs)
Use audited standard implementations rather than writing your own

blocks.text: A token does not 'live in your wallet' the way a file lives on your computer. A token is a **smart contract** that maintains a mapping of addresses to balances — a private little ledger of who owns how much. When you 'send 10 tokens to Bob,' nothing physically moves; the token contract simply subtracts 10 from your entry in its mapping and adds 10 to Bob's. Your wallet doesn't store the tokens; it stores your *keys*, and it reads your balance from the token contract. This is the mental shift: a token is a program that keeps score, and 'owning' a token means the token contract's ledger has an entry crediting your address.

Because a token is just a contract's internal ledger, adding a token to your wallet is only telling the wallet which contract address to read. The tokens were already 'yours' on-chain; importing the address just lets the wallet display the balance. Nothing is transferred by adding a token to your wallet.

sections.heading: Standards: why every token speaks the same language

blocks.text: If every token contract had different function names, no wallet or exchange could support them all. **Standards** solve this. A token standard is an agreed **interface** — a fixed set of function names and events every conforming contract must provide. Because a token follows the standard, any wallet, exchange, or app that speaks that standard can use it without custom code. This interoperability is the reason tokens exploded: build to the standard and the entire ecosystem supports your token automatically. The standards are called **ERCs** (Ethereum Request for Comments); ERC-20 for interchangeable tokens and ERC-721 for unique ones are the two that matter most.

**ERC-20** is the standard for **fungible** tokens — tokens that are all identical and interchangeable, like currency: any one unit is worth exactly the same as any other. Stablecoins, governance tokens, and most 'coins' built on Ethereum are ERC-20. The standard defines a small interface: `totalSupply` (how many exist), `balanceOf(account)` (an account's balance), `transfer(to, amount)` (send your own tokens), plus an approval mechanism — `approve(spender, amount)` and `transferFrom(from, to, amount)` — that lets you authorise another contract to spend a set amount on your behalf, which is how you interact with exchanges and DeFi. Two events, `Transfer` and `Approval`, announce these actions so wallets can track them.

The **approve / transferFrom** pattern is worth understanding because it powers DeFi. You can't send tokens *into* another contract just by transferring; instead you `approve` that contract to withdraw up to some amount, and it then calls `transferFrom` to pull them when needed. This two-step 'allowance' is how a DEX or lending protocol moves your tokens with your permission but without holding your keys.

**ERC-721** is the standard for **non-fungible** tokens — each one is unique and not interchangeable. Where an ERC-20 tracks *how many* tokens each address holds, an ERC-721 tracks *which specific token* (by a unique `tokenId`) each address owns. That's the essence of an NFT: a ledger mapping each unique id to an owner. The interface centres on `ownerOf(tokenId)` (who owns a specific token) and `balanceOf(owner)` (how many an address owns), with `transferFrom` and `safeTransferFrom` to move a specific token. A `tokenURI(tokenId)` typically points to metadata — a name, an image link — usually stored off-chain (often on IPFS, a later lesson), because storing images on-chain would be enormously expensive.

A common misconception: the NFT is not the image. The NFT is the on-chain record of who owns tokenId 42; the image it points to almost always lives off-chain. This is why where the metadata is stored (and whether that storage is permanent) matters so much for an NFT's real durability.

You now understand what these standards require, which is exactly why you should reach for a **battle-tested implementation** rather than writing your own. **OpenZeppelin** publishes audited, widely used implementations of ERC-20, ERC-721, and more; you inherit from them and add only your specifics. Token contracts hold real value and a subtle bug is catastrophic and permanent, so re-implementing a standard yourself invites exactly the vulnerabilities audited libraries have already fixed. The professional pattern is to import the standard base, then extend it. Understanding the interface (this lesson) lets you use those libraries correctly and read what they do.

That whole token — name, symbol, transfers, approvals, events — comes from inheriting the audited ERC20 base; you wrote only the constructor. This is exactly what the first blockchain project builds and deploys. With standards understood, the next stage moves to the tooling that lets you compile, test, and deploy contracts like this one for real.

practice.title: Reason about tokens and standards
steps: Explain, using the mapping idea, what actually changes when you 'send' 10 ERC-20 tokens to someone.
List the core ERC-20 functions and say what each one does in a sentence.
Walk through the approve / transferFrom flow and explain why a DEX needs it instead of a plain transfer.
Explain the difference between ERC-20 and ERC-721 in terms of what their ledgers track.
Explain why you'd inherit from OpenZeppelin's ERC20 rather than implement the interface yourself.

focus: A token is a contract with a ledger of who owns what — nothing physically moves.
Standards are shared interfaces so every wallet and app can use any conforming token.
ERC-20 = fungible (interchangeable) tokens; ERC-721 = non-fungible (unique) tokens.
ERC-20's approve/transferFrom allowance is how DeFi moves your tokens with permission.
An NFT is the on-chain ownership record; its image/metadata usually lives off-chain.
Inherit audited implementations (OpenZeppelin); never re-implement a standard by hand.

items.desc: a mapping of address to balance
your wallet stores keys, not tokens
the NFT is the ownership record
standards are easy to get wrong

pitfalls: Thinking tokens physically move or live in the wallet — the wallet just reads a contract's ledger.
Trying to send ERC-20 tokens into a contract with transfer instead of the approve/transferFrom flow.
Believing an NFT contains the image; the media almost always lives off-chain.
Storing large data or images on-chain, which is enormously expensive.
Re-implementing ERC-20 or ERC-721 by hand instead of inheriting an audited base.

quiz.q: What actually happens when you 'send' ERC-20 tokens to someone?
options: A file representing the tokens is copied to their device
The token contract updates its ledger: less for you, more for them
The tokens are physically moved out of your wallet app
A brand-new token contract is deployed for the recipient
quiz.explain: A token is a contract with a mapping of balances; a transfer just decreases your entry and increases theirs. Nothing physically moves and the wallet only stores your keys.

quiz.q: Why do token standards like ERC-20 exist?
options: To make tokens run faster than plain ether transfers
So any wallet or app can use any conforming token
To keep each token's balances completely private
To let one company control which tokens are allowed
quiz.explain: A standard is a shared interface, so wallets, exchanges and apps can support any token that follows it without custom code — the interoperability that made tokens ubiquitous.

quiz.q: What is the difference between ERC-20 and ERC-721?
options: ERC-20 is fungible (interchangeable); ERC-721 is unique per token
ERC-20 is for images and ERC-721 is for currencies
ERC-721 is simply an older version of ERC-20
There is no real difference between the two standards
quiz.explain: ERC-20 tokens are all identical and interchangeable like currency; ERC-721 tokens each have a unique tokenId and owner, making them non-fungible (NFTs).

quiz.q: What does the approve / transferFrom pattern enable?
options: Sending tokens without paying any gas fee
Authorising a contract to spend a set amount of your tokens
Permanently freezing another user's token balance
Converting an ERC-20 token into an ERC-721 token
quiz.explain: You approve a spender (like a DEX) for an amount, and it later calls transferFrom to pull those tokens with your permission — the allowance mechanism that powers DeFi.

quiz.q: Why inherit from OpenZeppelin instead of writing a token from scratch?
options: It is the only way a token can compile at all
Its implementations are audited, so you avoid known bugs
Home-made tokens are banned by the Ethereum network
OpenZeppelin tokens are exempt from paying gas fees
quiz.explain: Token contracts hold real value and subtle bugs are catastrophic and permanent; inheriting an audited implementation avoids the vulnerabilities that hand-rolled standards invite.
